name: Khorovats
summary: Armenian-style barbecue: meat grilled over fire, often with smoky aubergines, tomatoes and peppers. Pork and beef are popular choices, with plenty of variations from cook to cook.
tradition: An outdoor meal that brings family and friends together around the grill.
fact: Khorovats means ‘grilled’. Vegetables can be stars of the barbecue, too!
imageAlt: Armenian khorovats skewers grilling over coals in Sevan

name: Tolma / Dolma
diet: Meat or vegetarian; check the filling
summary: Grape leaves, cabbage leaves or vegetables filled with seasoned rice and minced meat. Meat-free pasuts tolma uses legumes and grains; the photograph shows a cabbage-and-legume version.
ingredients: Grape or cabbage leaves, or vegetables
Beans, lentils and chickpeas in pasuts tolma
tradition: Served for guests and celebrations. Pasuts tolma is associated with Lent and also appears on New Year tables.
fact: Stuffed dishes are shared across neighboring cuisines. Eastern Armenian commonly uses ‘tolma’; Western Armenian also uses ‘dolma’.
imageAlt: Cabbage-wrapped vegetarian tolma filled with legumes

name: Lavash
summary: A thin, flexible flatbread that can wrap cheese, greens or grilled meat. Traditional Armenian bakers stretch the dough onto a cushion and press it against the hot wall of a clay tonir oven.
tradition: Lavash-making is a shared family and community skill. At some Armenian weddings, bread is placed on the newlyweds’ shoulders as a wish for prosperity.
fact: UNESCO recognized Armenia’s lavash-making cultural tradition in 2014. Related flatbread traditions are also practiced and recognized elsewhere in the region.
imageAlt: Folded sheets of thin Armenian lavash bread

name: Harissa
summary: A thick, comforting porridge of wheat and meat, slowly cooked and stirred until the ingredients blend together. Chicken is common today; lamb is another traditional choice.
tradition: Long cooking and shared stirring make harissa a communal dish, enjoyed at religious observances and cultural gatherings.
fact: Armenian harissa is a wheat-and-meat dish. The similarly named North African chili paste is a different food.
imageAlt: A bowl of Armenian wheat-and-meat harissa topped with butter

name: Ghapama
diet: Vegetarian; usually contains butter and honey
summary: A whole pumpkin filled with rice, dried fruit and nuts, then baked until tender. Its sweet and savory filling makes the opened pumpkin a colorful centerpiece.
tradition: Made for festive tables and larger groups; it also appears at autumn harvest celebrations.
fact: Ghapama even has a song celebrating it: ‘Hey Jan, Ghapama’!
imageAlt: Baked ghapama pumpkins being opened at Lavash Restaurant in Yerevan

name: Gata
diet: Vegetarian; contains dairy and often egg
summary: A golden Armenian sweet pastry or sweet bread with many regional shapes and textures. A familiar filling is khoriz: a crumbly mixture of flour, sugar and butter; some recipes add walnuts.
ingredients: Egg or dairy in many doughs
tradition: Enjoyed with tea or coffee and baked for family occasions. Regional recipes range from large round breads to layered slices.
fact: There is no single look for gata: its shape, filling and dough vary around Armenia.
imageAlt: Golden slices of Armenian gata pastry on a plate

sources.label: Smithsonian — For the Love of Lavash

name: Spas
diet: Vegetarian version shown; contains dairy and often egg
summary: A tangy yogurt-based soup with wheat and fragrant herbs. Family recipes differ: some use buttermilk, some yogurt, and others include rice or barley instead of wheat.
ingredients: Egg and flour in many recipes
tradition: Everyday comfort food with regional variations, including tanov spas in Lori. It can be served warm or chilled.
fact: Gentle heating and stirring help keep the dairy smooth; egg and flour often help prevent curdling.
imageAlt: A bowl of white Armenian yogurt and grain soup, spas

name: Jingalov Hats / Zhingyalov Hats
summary: Thin flatbread packed with chopped greens and herbs, sealed and cooked on a hot griddle. The filling balances mild, aromatic and pleasantly sour leaves.
tradition: Strongly associated with the Armenian food traditions of Artsakh / Nagorno-Karabakh and Syunik; the greens change with the season.
fact: A single filling may combine 10–20 kinds of greens. Transliteration varies, so you may see several spellings of its name.
imageAlt: Jingalov hats, a flatbread filled with green herbs

name: Khash
summary: A rich broth made by slowly simmering carefully cleaned cow’s feet and related cuts. At the table, garlic and pieces of dried lavash are familiar additions.
tradition: In Armenia, cold-season khash breakfasts are long, sociable gatherings that often begin early in the morning.
fact: Khash turns lengthy simmering into a shared breakfast ritual. Related soups are found across the Caucasus and neighboring regions.
imageAlt: Armenian khash broth in a clay bowl with traditional table accompaniments

name: Sweet Sujukh / Sharots
summary: Walnuts threaded onto a string, dipped in thickened fruit syrup and dried into a chewy confection. Grape juice is common; other fruit-based versions also exist.
ingredients: Grape juice or other fruit syrup
tradition: An Armenian market sweet that reflects traditions of preserving nuts and fruit. Similar confections are also enjoyed in neighboring cuisines.
fact: Ask for ‘sweet’ sujukh: the word sujukh can also refer to a savory sausage!
imageAlt: Strings of sweet walnut sujukh for sale near Garni, Armenia

name: Armenian Coffee
summary: Strong, finely ground coffee gently brewed in a small pot called a jazzve, then served in a little cup. The grounds settle at the bottom, so sip slowly.
tradition: A familiar companion to conversation and breakfast, alongside Armenia’s lively modern café culture.
fact: This brewing style is shared across the region and goes by different names. ‘Armenian coffee’ describes its local tradition, rather than an exclusive invention.
imageAlt: A small cup of Armenian black coffee on a saucer
